title: What Cosmic Tree is for
subtitle: A bot that knocked on the same door six times

lines: Here's what happened.
We built a bot with Grok to help us run our Discord server. Its very first task was to open Discord's website.
It knocked six times. Six times the connection dropped.
It could not get in. We still don't know why.
Then it found another door, the official API Discord keeps for bots.
The front door stayed shut no matter how hard it knocked.
Through the side door it created channels, posted messages, pinned them. Everything worked.
Nobody had told it in advance which door to use.
We have run into this ourselves.
A game page we built opens to three digits on a phone in mainland China: 401.
It is not that AI can't get in. Nobody in mainland China can, humans included.
Another time, an AI was posting feedback on GitHub for us.
It did everything itself, right up to the Send button.
Then it stopped and came back to ask: send or not?
We said send it. Under a minute.
It went back and sent it.

params.bubble: Go get a few things done for me

lines: Think about it. This will only happen more.
Shopping, finding videos, research, posting. More and more errands on the web are run by AI.
But the web was built for people. Every time the AI gets stuck, a person has to stop and help.
So we set out to do something a little stubborn: measure the whole web by how hard it is for AI to get in.
One card per platform: can the AI get in, where does it get stuck, which step needs a human.
The cards live in a public GitHub repository called Cosmic Tree.
Each card has two scores, both out of 100.
Friendliness: how much road the platform paved for AI. Our own repository scores {f:opc-cosmic-tree}.
Anti-agent: how many walls it put up on purpose. Ours scores {a:opc-cosmic-tree}.
Honestly, one number matters even more than the two scores: time.
How many times, and for how many minutes, a person had to step in. Run the same task three times, keep the middle one.
Ours came out at zero minutes all three times; it just needed a nod. That number is the real cost to you.

params.title: How we test
items: No IP rotation, no posing as anyone
No money from the platforms we rate

lines: One thing to be clear about: we only do what any normal user could do.
A CAPTCHA means we stop. We never get around it.
No IP rotation, no posing as someone else, no borrowed accounts.
Every score comes with the raw records from that moment.
And we take no money from the platforms we rate.
We rate websites ourselves, one by one, and keep the repository updated.
Before your AI goes somewhere, it checks first. If the site is rated, it just reads the card.
Or install our skill and test your own task. Send the result back if you like, or keep it.
Want a site rated first? Open a request in the repository.
One catch: the same site opens different doors for different tasks.
On GitHub, anyone can read a public repository.
Opening an issue needs a login.
Merging into someone else's repository needs a login and their permission.
So difficulty depends on the task. An AI can walk its own chain of tasks with the skill.
Results sent back stay public: who sent them, and when.
The skill stamps a fingerprint so everyone reports the same way.
Our AI walks the key steps again from the record, and only matching results go in.

params.title: Create a Discord channel
items: Use the official API, not the website
Don't mix up the two keys
params.added: Found a new trap? Add a dated line.

lines: One more piece we haven't built yet, but really want to: not just where AI gets stuck, but how to get it done.
To create a Discord channel, skip the website and use the official API.
The two keys look alike. Mix them up and you get a 401.
Creating channels needs a permission only the owner can grant.
Whoever finds a new trap adds a dated line.
Back to that bot. If it had checked Cosmic Tree first, it would not have knocked six times.
That's Cosmic Tree. {cards} leaves today, {rated} of them lit.
The rest are waiting for your AI.

ending: Next time you send an AI on an errand, it checks first: can it get in, where will it get stuck, what's the smoothest way, and when will it need you.
